## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- "Charge" translates a strong Greek word (*diamarturomai*), elsewhere rendered "testified." Paul is giving Timothy solemn testimony he must heed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-4/ 
- Ellicott: thinking ahead to judgment day should spur on a discouraged servant who is tempted to compromise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm 
- Ellicott on the Greek text: older manuscripts read "and" instead of "at." That makes the phrase an oath formula: "I charge you *by* His appearing and *by* His kingdom." He notes this harder reading actually makes the verse stronger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm
- Gill: "the living and the dead" means those still alive at Christ's coming and those raised from the dead. Together they include everyone, all of whom must stand before Christ's judgment seat. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_timothy/4.htm 

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: "preach" means proclaim openly and loudly, as a herald announces a new king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm 
- Ellicott on "in season and out of season": ministry has no fixed hours. It goes on in danger, in chains, even under threat of death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm 
- Gill: rebuke is to be fitted to the case, sometimes in private and sometimes in public, sometimes gently and sometimes sharply. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/4-2.html 
- Gill: patience means waiting for results the way a farmer waits for a harvest. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/4-2.html 
- Ellicott: correction and comfort must always come with sound teaching. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm 

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: people would increasingly want new teaching that eases a troubled conscience while letting them keep living self-indulgently. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm 
- Gill: the warning was about the future when Paul wrote, but it came true soon. He says its marks have shown up in every age, including his own. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-timothy-4.html 
- Bob Utley (bible.org): the warning applies to Paul's day, in some sense to every day, and especially to the last days. https://bible.org/seriespage/2-timothy-4 

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: turning away from the truth was the punishment for listening only to flattery. Such people ended up rejecting every Christian truth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm 
- Gill: the "myths" may mean Jewish fables or pagan and Gnostic mythologies. More broadly, they cover anything empty and pointless, and he sees being handed over to them as God's judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_timothy/4.htm

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: "be sober" means keep a cool head and stay alert. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm
- Ellicott: early "evangelists" seem to have been gospel preachers who assisted the apostles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm 
- Bible.org (Lesson 19) paraphrases the command as: don't quit the ministry for easier work just because you meet opposition. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-19-preaching-and-hearing-god%E2%80%99s-word-2-timothy-41-5 

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: in Philippians 2:17 Paul spoke of martyrdom as a possibility. Here he writes as if it has already begun. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm 
- Ellicott: the word for "departure" can mean a ship raising anchor and slipping its moorings. Utley adds that this noun occurs only here in the New Testament. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm and https://bible.org/seriespage/2-timothy-4 
- Guzik: there may also be a Roman picture here. Roman meals ended by pouring out a cup of wine to the gods. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-4/ 
- Gill: Paul's death is no atoning sacrifice. Christ's death is the only sacrifice for sin, and it is complete. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_timothy/4.htm

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: the image is an athlete in the games. Paul's "course" is the ministry he received from the Lord (Acts 20:24). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm
- Ellicott: "kept the faith" pictures guarding a treasure and passing it on safely. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm 
- Gill: "the faith" mainly means the doctrine entrusted to Paul, though it may also mean his faithfulness as a steward. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_timothy/4.htm

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: "the righteous Judge" probably contrasts with the unjust Roman judge who condemned Paul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm 
- Guzik: this is the victor's crown (*stephanos*), a trophy, not a royal crown. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-4/ 
- Ellicott: the same crown is offered to all who truly long for Christ's return. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm 
- Utley: Paul apparently believed believers are with the Lord at death, but full rewards wait for Resurrection Day. https://bible.org/seriespage/2-timothy-4 

**v. 9**
- Gill: Paul wanted more than company. He had matters about the churches to discuss face to face. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-timothy-4.html 
- Guzik: Paul was not superhuman. He was lonely and wanted companionship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-4/ 

**v. 10**
- Guzik: people left Paul for different reasons. Demas loved the world, Crescens and Titus left out of necessity, and Tychicus was sent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-4/ 
- David Mathis (Desiring God): Demas had once been a faithful partner (Colossians 4). Paul probably wanted Timothy warned by why Demas left. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-sadness-and-beauty-of-pauls-final-words 

**v. 11**
- Guzik: Luke stayed. This is a sharp contrast with Paul's first Roman imprisonment, when he had many visitors (Acts 28:30–31). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-4/ 
- Ellicott: Luke was probably writing this letter as Paul dictated. Utley also suggests Luke served as scribe for these letters. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm and https://bible.org/seriespage/2-timothy-4 

**v. 12**
- Guzik places Tychicus among those Paul sent away, not those who deserted him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-4/

**v. 13**
- Mathis: being close to God at the end of life doesn't remove the need to read. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-sadness-and-beauty-of-pauls-final-words 
- Mathis also draws the lesson that people with great influence don't need great possessions. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-sadness-and-beauty-of-pauls-final-words 

**v. 14**
- Gill: probably the same Alexander as in the Ephesus riot and in 1 Timothy 1:20. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-timothy-4.html 
- Guzik: Alexander may have been an informer who betrayed Paul to Rome, or a witness against him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-4/ 
- Paul Jeon (TGC): Paul leaves Alexander to God's justice instead of acting himself. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/2-timothy/ 

**v. 15**
- Gill: the warning is mainly about Alexander's opposition to the gospel, not the personal harm he did Paul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-timothy-4.html 

**v. 16**
- Gill: Paul treats these people differently from Alexander. They failed out of weakness; Alexander acted out of malice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_timothy/4.htm 
- Mathis calls this possibly the saddest sentence in the letter. He notes that imperfect friends can still be friends. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-sadness-and-beauty-of-pauls-final-words  
- Guzik: Paul's lack of bitterness shows real spiritual maturity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-4/ 

**v. 17**
- Guzik: Paul stood alone, but Jesus stood by him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-4/ 
- Guzik: Paul didn't know whether this time would end in rescue or in being kept for the heavenly kingdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-4/ 

**v. 18**
- Guzik: Paul's praise shows unlikely joy. He was possibly poor, cold and friendless, yet would trade places with no one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-4/ 

**v. 19**
- Guzik: Paul's final thoughts were for others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-4/ 

**v. 20**
- Ellicott (quoted on Biblehub): Trophimus had once been the reason Paul was arrested in Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/2_timothy/4-20.htm 
- Meyer (on Biblehub): Paul did not pass through Miletus before his first Roman imprisonment, so this verse supports a second imprisonment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_timothy/4-20.htm 

**v. 21**
- Poole: "before winter" because winter sailing was dangerous, or because Paul would need more help then. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_timothy/4-21.htm 
- Bengel: Timothy could take courage from the fact that the friends named were still alive. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_timothy/4-21.htm 

**v. 22**
- Guzik's study guide quotes a commentator who sees here a prayer for a close personal bond between the Lord and Timothy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/studyguide_2ti/2ti_4.cfm

## Where Protestant teachers differ

**v. 1: what "His kingdom" means**
- Gill (a Baptist; that label is mine) reads it as Christ's personal thousand-year reign. Saints are judged at its start and the wicked at its end. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_timothy/4.htm
- Ellicott (Anglican; my label) reads it as the kingdom that "shall have no end," as the Nicene Creed puts it. He finds the beginnings of the ancient creeds in this verse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_timothy/4.htm

**v. 8: is the crown earned?**
- Calvin (Reformed; my label) says Catholics use this verse to build a doctrine of merit against grace, and calls their reasoning "absurd." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/4-8.html 
- Thomas Watson (Puritan, on monergism.com) says we cannot earn this crown by our own righteousness. https://www.monergism.com/crown-righteousness 
- Poole says Christ gives it freely, because nothing Paul did deserved it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_timothy/4-8.htm 
- Adam Clarke takes a different line. Paul can claim the crown as his due: a reward God promised to those who stay faithful to the grace He gave them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/4-8.html 
- The Biblehub study note says the righteousness is credited through faith, not self-made. https://biblehub.com/study/2_timothy/4-8.htm 
- Precept Austin presents the crown as Christ's righteousness given in full to the glorified believer. It ties "that day" to the Judgment Seat of Christ, where rewards are given. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_47-8 

**v. 5: what an evangelist preaches**
- Gill insists it means preaching salvation by grace alone, not moral lectures or mixing law and gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_timothy/4.htm

## Other views

**v. 21: Linus (Catholic reading)**
- The Catholic Encyclopedia says Irenaeus identified Pope Linus with the Linus of this verse. It frankly admits it can't be sure whether that identification goes back to a reliable source or arose from the shared name. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/09272b.htm  
- Catholic Answers cites Eusebius as testifying that this Linus succeeded Peter as bishop of Rome. https://www.catholic.com/qa/evidence-that-linus-succeeded-peter-as-pope 
- Ellicott accepts that Linus was the first bishop of Rome. Bengel notes he is listed third, so he was not yet a bishop when Paul wrote. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_timothy/4-21.htm  
- Gill uses the early disagreement over Peter's immediate successor to argue against the claimed papal succession. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-timothy-4.html 

**v. 20: does God always heal? (aimed at "health for all" teaching)**
- None of the sources I found names prosperity or word-of-faith teaching directly. These pages respond to the idea that healing is always God's will.
- Spurgeon: Paul could have healed Trophimus if the Spirit had allowed it, but it was God's will that he be ill. He adds that sickness is not always caused by personal sin. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/the-sick-man-left-behind/  
- GotQuestions criticizes the view that healing is proof of a person's faith. https://www.gotquestions.org/God-heal-everyone.html 
- Clarke: even apostles could not work miracles whenever they wanted. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/4-20.html 
- Constable says healing always depended on God's sovereign will. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/4-20.html 
- Coffman argues miracles were never done for private benefit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/4-20.html 

**Date and setting**
- Utley dates the letter to around A.D. 67–68, written as Paul's last before his martyrdom. https://bible.org/seriespage/2-timothy-4 
- I found no modern-scholarship pages taking a different view on authorship or date.
